3.2.3.1-f101.accuracy_reason: Georgics 4.465–66 reads 'secum ... decedente canebat', so Burton has made the lines first person.

3.2.3.1-f105.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.9.10–12, addressed to Valgius, reads 'nec tibi Vespero'.

3.2.3.1-f108.accuracy_reason: This is [Tibullus] 3.3.25–26, part of the Lygdamus poems (3.1–6).

3.2.3.1-f110.accuracy_reason: Clitophon is the narrator and lover of Leucippe in Achilles Tatius, and Burton cites the romance in Latin translation.

3.2.3.1-f112.accuracy_reason: Aen. 4.4, 'haerent infixi pectore vultus', refers to Aeneas' looks fixed in Dido's heart.

3.2.3.1-f117.accuracy_reason: Amores 1.9 opens 'Militat omnis amans, et habet sua castra Cupido', and the poem compares love to soldiering.

3.2.3.1-f118.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.2 reads 'caeco carpitur igni' and is about Dido. Eclogue 3.66 reads 'at mihi sese offert ultro, meus ignis, Amyntas'.

3.2.3.1-f119.accuracy_reason: Terence, Eunuchus 85, reads 'accede ad ignem hunc, iam calesces plus satis'. Ignis is masculine, so 'hanc' is an anomaly.

3.2.3.1-f121.accuracy_reason: This renders Theocritus, Idyll 2.133–4, on Eros kindling a flame hotter than Liparaean Hephaestus. Tradition placed Vulcan's forge in the Lipari islands.

3.2.3.1-f129.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.86–9 describes Carthage's building works stopping while Dido is in love. Reading machina as a crane or derrick is standard.

3.2.3.1-f138.accuracy_reason: Abelard's epitaph includes 'Huic soli patuit scibile quicquid erat'. Burton writes 'Cui'.

3.2.3.1-f141.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 3 m.12, reads 'Quis legem det amantibus? / Maior lex amor est sibi'.

3.2.3.1-f148.accuracy_reason: 'Amare et sapere vix deo conceditur' is among Publilius Syrus's sententiae, which circulated under Seneca's name. Burton's attribution is therefore explicable.

3.2.3.1-f151.accuracy_reason: Seneca's Phaedra 184–5 reads 'quid ratio possit? vicit ac regnat furor, / potensque tota mente dominatur deus'.

3.2.3.1-f152.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.319–21, continues 'di, precor, et pietas sacrataque iura parentum', so the summary of the omitted prayer is right.

3.2.3.1-f156.accuracy_reason: In the Golden Ass, Lucius regains his human form by eating roses, and an allegorical reading as a return to reason is standard.

3.2.3.1-f161.accuracy_reason: Metamorphoses 1.502 reads 'si qua latent, meliora putat', said of Apollo looking at Daphne. Burton's 'puta' is an imperative.

3.2.3.1-f173.accuracy_reason: Catullus 25 opens 'Cinaede Thalle, mollior cuniculi capillo', mocking the effeminate Thallus. Burton does apply the phrase to the mistress.

3.2.3.1-f177.accuracy_reason: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.789ff, Polyphemus sings 'floridior pratis', and lines are skipped before 'mollior et cycni plumis'. Burton's English does give 'withywind'.

3.2.3.1-f184.accuracy_reason: Cypris is Venus, and Stratonice was a Seleucid queen famed for her beauty. In his English gloss Burton puts the Spanish Infanta in her place.

3.2.3.1-f185.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Martial 5.37 (Erotion), which older editions numbered 38, matching Burton's sidenote. The transmitted text reads 'erat'.

3.2.3.1-f186.accuracy_reason: This is Catulus's epigram on Roscius, which Cicero preserves at De natura deorum 1.79.

3.2.3.1-f190.accuracy_reason: Margareta/margarita ('pearl') is a natural pun, and the following 'pretiosa' supports it.

3.2.3.1-f192.accuracy_reason: The line is [Tibullus] 4.2.14, one of the Sulpicia poems.

3.2.3.1-f195.accuracy_reason: Aristaenetus Epist. 1.1 has ἐνδέδυται… εὐπροσωποτάτη· ἐκδέδυται… ὅλη πρόσωπον. The Latin keeps the wordplay with formosa/forma.

3.2.3.1-f207.accuracy_reason: At Aeneid 1.76–77 Aeolus is speaking to Juno, and the standard text reads 'quid optes'.

3.2.3.1-f213.accuracy_reason: In Martial, Spectacula 25b (28 in some editions), the line reads 'mergite cum redeo'.

3.2.3.1-f220.accuracy_reason: Martial 1.71 begins 'Laevia sex cyathis, septem Iustina bibatur', and that poem describes the custom of a cup per letter.

3.2.3.1-f227.accuracy_reason: In Horace, Odes 1.9.23–24, the girl only pretends to resist, so 'male pertinaci' means 'hardly holding on'.

3.2.3.1-f235.accuracy_reason: Catullus 2.9–10 is identified correctly, and 'O si' does appear to be Burton's addition. But in Catullus the lines are already a wish ('possem', a subjunctive of wishing), so saying Burton added 'O si' 'to turn the lines into a wish' is misleading.

3.2.3.1-f247.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 79 reads 'Qualis nox fuit illa, di deaeque, / quam mollis torus', so Burton's 'erit' does make it future.

3.2.3.1-f250.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 4.429 does read 'det', so that point is right. Nothing in the text given confirms that the woman pleading is 'the Sultan's wife'; this needs checking against Burton's source.

3.2.3.1-f252.accuracy_reason: Met. 4.187–8 reads 'aliquis de dis non tristibus optat / sic fieri turpis', so the note has both the story and the verb right.

3.2.3.1-f254.accuracy_reason: Horace Odes 3.9 has 'pro qua non metuam mori' and 'pro quo bis patiar mori', so the note's account of the combination is accurate.

3.2.3.1-f260.accuracy_reason: Met. 4.96 says 'audacem faciebat amor' of Thisbe.

3.2.3.1-f268.accuracy_reason: At Aeneid 4.296 Dido senses Aeneas' plan to leave ('quis fallere possit amantem?'). Burton does apply it to the cunning of love.

3.2.3.1-f29.accuracy_reason: The line closes the Petronian poem 'Foeda est in coitu et brevis voluptas', which prefers kisses and lingering embraces to the act itself.

3.2.3.1-f297.accuracy_reason: This is a Latin version of Mimnermus fr. 1 ('What is life, what delight, without golden Aphrodite? May I die…'). Burton's English gives only the second sentence, and loosely.

3.2.3.1-f305.accuracy_reason: The epigram is Martial 8.73, not book 9 as the sidenote has it. The Pelignian land is Ovid's homeland and Mantua Virgil's; Corinna and Alexis are their beloveds.

3.2.3.1-f311.accuracy_reason: Verrines 2.3.76 describes the Persian and Syrian kings giving cities to their wives in this way.

3.2.3.1-f314.accuracy_reason: Socrates talks in the Piraeus (Republic) and the Lyceum (Euthydemus), and under the plane tree in the Phaedrus.

3.2.3.1-f316.accuracy_reason: The full line is right (Terence, Heauton Timorumenos 77), and the note describes Burton's use of it correctly.

3.2.3.1-f317.accuracy_reason: Ovid does call himself 'praeceptor Amoris' (Ars Amatoria 1.17). The note rightly hedges the exact wording.

3.2.3.1-f322.accuracy_reason: Apuleius, Met. 10.2 goes on 'lassa genua, quies turbida, et suspiritus...'. Burton's 'restless thoughts, short wind' do render items past where his Latin stops.

3.2.3.1-f336.accuracy_reason: This is the correct scholastic sense of anima informans: the soul as substantial form.

3.2.3.1-f34.accuracy_reason: The Catullus 5.7–9 readings are given correctly. Burton's own sidenote supports the statement that the English is Jonson's imitation.

3.2.3.1-f372.accuracy_reason: It is an Erasmus adage, and it goes back to Euripides (Stheneboea fr., quoted in Plato's Symposium 196e).

3.2.3.1-f379.accuracy_reason: Josephus, Ant. 18.66–80: Decius Mundus, of equestrian rank, offered Paulina 200,000 drachmae.

3.2.3.1-f40.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 4.1079–81 has 'premunt arte... dentes inlidunt saepe labellis / osculaque adfigunt'. The note hedges suitably on both the slip and the compression.

3.2.3.1-f426.accuracy_reason: The line is Ovid, Heroides 15.79 (Sappho to Phaon), and the note quotes it correctly. It is not from Theocritus.

3.2.3.1-f436.accuracy_reason: Alphitomancy is correctly derived from alphiton and defined as divination by barley-meal. The note fairly observes that Burton's gloss about beans in a cake describes a folk custom.

3.2.3.1-f48.accuracy_reason: Anacreon fr. 360 PMG calls the beloved the one who 'holds the reins of my soul' (charioteer). The note paraphrases it fairly.

3.2.3.1-f54.accuracy_reason: The line is Martial 9.59.3, from the epigram about Mamurra.

3.2.3.1-f6.accuracy_reason: The lines are from Seneca's Phaedra (379–380). Phaedra is the daughter of Pasiphae, who was the daughter of the Sun, so the note's line of descent is right.

3.2.3.1-f62.accuracy_reason: The note quotes Plautus, Cistellaria 69–70, correctly and shows how Burton shortens it.

3.2.3.1-f68.accuracy_reason: The Terence (Eunuchus 59–61) and the Plautus (Mercator, from Charinus' opening speech) are rightly identified. Plautus does read 'incogitantia', and 'aviditas' is the correct form.

3.2.3.1-f70.accuracy_reason: In Hesiod's Theogony (933–936), Phobos and Deimos are the children of Ares and Aphrodite. The note's description is right.

3.2.3.1-f79.accuracy_reason: These are indeed the last two lines of Catullus 107.

3.2.3.1-f93.accuracy_reason: In Ptolemaic astronomy the primum mobile was the outermost sphere, which carried the spheres below it round.
